question: When a machine takes over a job's name and its routine tasks, what happens to the people in that job, and can the newest workers still find a way in?

issues.note: Hard cut from the programmers' classroom to an empty brick billboard with a blank dark panel. For about 2 s nothing is on it, and the caption 'a large occupation of its own' has no picture to match.

Jump from the classroom to the dusk lamplighter street with a lit window. The narration 'The lamplighter...' is a metaphor with no setup, and the look switches from the 1950s interior to a stylised exterior.
The dusk street cuts straight to a dark modern night office with monitors. The 'third kind of work' caption only arrives after the cut, so the change of era and look is abrupt.

The 'where will the next beginners learn?' shot is a dark, nearly unreadable close-up of a ladder base. It then cuts to the dusk street for 'What happens to a job...'. The picture does not match the question.

The 1990 BLS handbook is narrated over the reel-to-tape machine, then a quote card. The picture does not show what the narration says. The previous billboard says '519,000' under a caption about a count from another era, which is hard to follow.
The billboard sits on a static '519,000' for about 12 s (R10.1 to R10.3) with only the captions changing.
The billboard is static and nearly empty, then '-19%' stays on screen for about 20 s (R14.1 to R14.7). Only the captions change.
The same dark desk, monitor and lamp frame stays for about 16 s (R12.5 to R12.8) with only the captions changing.
The dark office with the lone desk repeats across R13.5 to R13.7 and again in R14.8 and R15.1. The picture is unchanged, only the captions move.
The same typewriter-and-graph desk close-up is used for R03.1, R03.2, R03.7 and R03.8 (about 4 to 8 s each time). It is the film's default shot and gets repetitive.
